entries.narration: Python is a general purpose programming language, and before writing a line of it, it is worth knowing what kind of language it is, because the five words across the top of the screen explain most of what you will meet in this course. It is high level: you describe what you want done, and Python takes care of how the machine does it. It is interpreted: a program called the interpreter reads your code and runs it, with no separate build step in between. It is dynamically typed: a name can refer to any kind of object, and the kind is checked while the program runs. It manages memory for you, freeing objects as soon as nothing uses them. And it comes with batteries included, a large standard library that you get the moment you install it. Below that is where Python actually runs, and the range is the point. The same language serves web back ends, through frameworks like Django and FastAPI. It is the everyday tool of data analysis, with pandas and Jupyter notebooks. Most machine learning is written in it. It automates servers and chores, and it moves data between systems in pipelines, which is exactly what we will build. It is also, very often, the first language people learn. At the bottom is one more distinction worth knowing early. Python is a language, and CPython is the program that runs it: the reference implementation, written in C. Others exist, but CPython is what you get from python dot org, and everything in this course, every number and every error message, was produced on CPython three point fifteen point one. Next, where this language came from.

Python is older than most people expect. In December nineteen eighty nine, Guido van Rossum started it as a holiday project at C W I, a research institute in Amsterdam, and the name comes from Monty Python's Flying Circus, not from the snake. The first public release came in February nineteen ninety one, already with classes, exceptions, functions, lists and dictionaries, and version one followed in nineteen ninety four. The second era began with Python two, in October two thousand, which brought list comprehensions and a garbage collector that could find cycles. The year after, the Python Software Foundation was formed to own the language. Then, in December two thousand and eight, Python three made a deliberate break with the past, to fix how text and division worked. The break was right, but it was slow: Python two was only retired in January twenty twenty, more than eleven years later. Everything in this course is Python three. The third era is the one you are joining. In two thousand eighteen Guido stepped down as the language's lead, and an elected Steering Council now guides it. Since three point nine in twenty twenty, a new version arrives every October. Three point eleven made CPython about a quarter faster on average. Three point thirteen offered an experimental build without the global interpreter lock, and three point fourteen made that build officially supported. And in October twenty twenty six, three point fifteen added lazy imports, a frozen dictionary type, and UTF eight as the default text encoding. We will use all three. Next, the ideas that shaped the language.

Python has a philosophy, and it is short enough to print. Type import this, and Python prints the Zen of Python, nineteen lines by Tim Peters. The terminal shows the first seven. Beautiful is better than ugly. Explicit is better than implicit. Simple is better than complex. And the one that matters most for us: readability counts. The editor shows why, with one rule written twice: ten percent off an order of three bags or more. The first version fits on one line. It is correct, and the terminal shows that both versions print twenty seven. But to understand it, a reader has to decode b, p, a bare point nine, and a condition hidden inside a multiplication, all at once. The second version says the same thing in five short lines. The names say what the values are, a docstring states the rule in plain words, and the discount is an if, which is exactly how you would describe it out loud. Code is read far more often than it is written, by colleagues, by reviewers, and by you, six months later. Python's style is built around that reader, and so is this course. The other half of the philosophy is the table on the right. Batteries included means the standard library covers most everyday jobs, and our pipeline will need nothing else. Exact money comes from decimal. The shop's daily files are read with csv, and the catalogue with json. pathlib finds the files, sqlite three stores the results, datetime handles the dates, and logging records what happened. All of it ships with Python. Next, what Python is fast at, and what it is not.

Every language makes trade offs, and Python's are worth knowing before you rely on it. The script in the editor adds up a million numbers in two ways and times both. The first is a loop written in Python: start at zero, and add each number in turn. The second calls the built in function, sum. Both give the same answer. The terminal, and the chart on the right, show how long each took, and on this machine, sum was about five times faster. Your numbers will differ, because timings depend on the machine and on what else it is doing, but the gap will be there. The reason is the shape of the whole language. sum is written in C, and it runs at the speed of C. The loop runs in the Python virtual machine, which you will meet in a few minutes, one small instruction at a time, and every one of those instructions has a cost. The table turns that into a rule of thumb. Python is fast to write and to read, and that is usually the expensive part of software. Calling code written in C is fast, and much of Python's power comes from exactly that: the standard library, and libraries like NumPy. Waiting on files and networks is fine, because the waiting dominates. A tight loop in pure Python code is slow. And on the default build, threads doing CPU work run one at a time, for a reason we will measure in course eleven. None of this means you should guess. The professional habit, which we will practise later, is to measure first and change only what the measurement points at. Next, what we are going to build.

This course does not teach Python as a list of features. It builds one application, from an empty folder to a tested, packaged job that runs on a schedule, and each feature arrives at the moment the application needs it. Here it is. A small coffee roastery's shop writes one file of orders every day: who ordered which coffee, and how many bags. Alongside those files there is a catalogue of products and their prices, and later in the course, an orders service on the network as well. Those are the sources, at the top. Our pipeline reads them, in the stage called extract. It checks every row, keeping the good ones and reporting the bad ones instead of crashing or, worse, silently getting a number wrong. That is validate. It prices every line and applies the discounts, which is transform, and then it adds the results up by product, by day and by customer, which is aggregate. Finally it writes what it found: a report people can read, a summary other programs can read, and a small database that can be safely loaded again and again. That is load, and those are the outputs at the bottom. Under each stage you can see the course that builds it, and the Python it is built from. Every stage is plain Python, using only the standard library. Courses two to seven build that script, starting with a single file. The purple rail at the bottom is the second half of the course: the same pipeline, turned into a package, modelled with objects, tested, measured, sped up and shipped. Before we start, there is one more thing to understand: what happens when Python runs your code.

When you type python main dot py and press enter, a lot happens before your first line of output appears, and knowing the stages explains most of the errors you will ever see. Each stage on screen shows what it makes of a one line program that prints the word hi. The interpreter first reads the file as plain text, a sequence of characters. The tokenizer turns those characters into tokens: names, numbers, strings and operators, the words of the language. The parser then checks those tokens against Python's grammar and builds a syntax tree, a structure that records what the code means. If the grammar is broken, this is where it stops, with a SyntaxError, before a single line has run. Next the compiler turns the tree into bytecode: a list of small, simple instructions. For a module that your program imports, that bytecode is saved, so the work is not repeated next time. Finally, the virtual machine runs the bytecode, one instruction at a time, and that is when your code actually does things: printing, reading files, computing. Errors found here, like a NameError for a misspelt name, only appear when the program reaches the line that causes them. The red row sums it up: which stage finds an error decides what has already happened. The important thing is that none of this is hidden. The bottom row shows how to look at every stage yourself, using tools that ship with Python. python dash m tokenize prints the tokens. python dash m ast prints the syntax tree, and python dash m dis prints the bytecode. The saved bytecode lives in a folder called pycache. Over the next five sections we will look inside: the bytecode, the virtual machine, the call stack, and how Python keeps track of names and objects in memory.

Let us watch the compiler at work on the smallest useful function. pricing dot py, in the editor, defines line total, which multiplies a price by a quantity. A second file, main dot py, imports it and prints the total for three bags. Run it, and look at the explorer: a folder called pycache has appeared, holding a file whose name ends in cpython three fifteen dot pyc. That is the compiled bytecode of pricing dot py, saved because it was imported. The next run can skip compiling it, as long as the source has not changed. The script you run directly, main dot py, is compiled every time and never saved, and the version number in the file name means each version of Python keeps its own cache. The table at the bottom of the right hand pane collects those rules. This folder is safe to delete, and it never belongs in version control. The second command runs look dot py, which shows the stages in between for the expression price times quantity. First the tokens, at the top of the right hand pane: a name, an operator, and another name. Then the syntax tree, drawn below them: a binary operation, whose operator is multiplication, with a name on the left and a name on the right. Then the bytecode for line total, which the next table explains line by line. After a resume instruction that starts the function, one instruction pushes both arguments, price and quantity. Recent versions of Python fuse common pairs like this into a single instruction, which is why the name is so long. Then binary op multiplies the top two values, and return value hands back the result. Four instructions for one line of Python. Next, how the virtual machine runs them.

Python's virtual machine is a stack machine, and once you can picture the stack, bytecode stops being mysterious. Here line total takes a discount as well: price times quantity, minus the discount. Called with ten, three and two, the terminal shows it returns twenty eight. The second command prints its bytecode, and the diagram on the right follows the value stack through every instruction, with the top of the stack first. The first instruction loads two arguments, price and quantity, and pushes them, so the stack holds ten, with three on top. Binary op, multiply, takes the top two values off the stack, multiplies them, and pushes the result: now there is only thirty. The next instruction pushes the discount, two, on top of the thirty. Binary op, subtract, takes those two values off again, computes thirty minus two, and pushes twenty eight. Finally return value takes the top of the stack and gives it back to whoever called the function. That is the whole model. Every instruction takes its operands from the top of the stack and leaves its result there. There are no named registers to keep track of, which is part of what makes the compiler simple, and the machine portable. It also explains the speed difference from a few sections ago. Adding a million numbers in a Python loop means running instructions like these millions of times, each one checking what kind of objects it has been given before it can do any arithmetic. Calling sum runs one loop written in C. So far, our functions have run on their own. Next, what happens when one function calls another.

Every time a function is called, Python creates a frame for it: a small record holding that call's local variables, and the line it has reached. Frames are kept on the call stack, and orders dot py lets us look at it directly. The last line calls order total with an order of two bags. order total loops over the order and calls line total for each product. And inside line total, before returning, a loop prints every frame on the stack, using the inspect module. The terminal shows three frames, newest first: line total at line seven, order total at line fifteen, and the module itself at line nineteen, where the first call was made. The diagram on the right draws the same three frames. The top one, line total, is running, with its own sku and its own quantity. Below it, order total is paused, waiting for that call to come back. It has its own variables, including total, still zero, and a reference to the order dictionary out on the right. At the bottom is the module's frame, which holds the names defined at the top of the file: the prices dictionary, and the two functions. When line total returns, its frame is removed, popped off the stack, and order total carries on exactly where it paused, adding the result to its total. That is what the table at the bottom summarises. A call pushes a frame, a return pops it, and each frame's variables belong to that call alone, which is why two functions can both use a name like sku without interfering. It also explains tracebacks: when an error is not handled, Python prints this stack. Next, the objects those names refer to.

In Python, a variable is not a box that holds a value. It is a name that refers to an object, and getting this right early prevents a whole family of bugs later. identity dot py makes a list of two product codes and binds it to the name a. The next line, b equals a, does not copy anything. It binds a second name to the same object, which is what the top diagram on the right shows: two names, one arrow each, one list. The third line builds a new list with the same two codes, and binds it to c. That is a separate object that happens to hold equal values, shown in the second diagram. Every object has three things: an identity, a type and a value. The id function returns the identity, which in CPython is the object's address in memory. The terminal shows that a and b have the same id, and c has a different one. Your numbers will differ on every run, but that pattern will not. Python gives you two ways to compare. The is operator asks whether two names refer to the very same object, so a is b is true, and a is c is false. The double equals operator asks whether the values are equal, so a equals c is true as well. The first table below the diagrams puts those answers side by side, and the next one lists the three things that list has. In everyday code you almost always want double equals; is is for checking identity, most often against None. Remember b equals a. When we start changing lists and dictionaries in course three, a change made through one name will show up through the other. Next, how objects disappear.

If names refer to objects, something has to decide when an object is no longer needed, and in CPython that is mostly reference counting. Every object keeps a count of the references to it, and the moment that count reaches zero, the object is freed. refs dot py makes a dictionary for one order and asks sys dot getrefcount how many references it has. The answer is two: the name order, and the temporary reference created by passing it to the function itself. The table on the right records that explanation beside each number. Binding a second name, alias, raises the count to three, as the top diagram shows, and deleting alias brings it back to two. Note that del removes a name, not an object. The object only goes away when the last reference does. Reference counting has one blind spot. The second half of the file builds two dictionaries that refer to each other, a cycle, and then deletes both names. Nothing in the program can reach either dictionary any more, but each still holds a reference to the other, so neither count can fall to zero. That is the second diagram. For this, CPython also runs a garbage collector, which periodically looks for groups of objects that nothing else can reach. Calling gc dot collect runs it immediately, and it reports finding two unreachable objects: exactly our two dictionaries. You will rarely call it yourself. But this is why a long running program can hold on to memory you thought was released, and why course eleven measures memory instead of guessing. That completes the picture. Next, we start building the pipeline.

Every project in this course starts the same way, and so does ours: an empty folder, and a Python of its own. In the terminal, we make a folder called roastery etl and step into it. Then one command, python three point fifteen, dash m, venv, dot venv, creates a virtual environment, a folder named dot venv inside the project. It prints nothing, but look at the explorer on the left: dot venv now holds a bin folder, a lib folder, and a small file called pyvenv dot cfg, open in the editor. Its first line says where this environment came from: the Python installed in user local. Back in the terminal, the first which python answers user local. Then we activate the environment, and the same question gets a different answer: the python inside dot venv. Activating does nothing more mysterious than putting that folder first on your path. The diagram on the right shows what you really have. The environment's python is not a second copy of Python; readlink shows it is a link to the one interpreter in user local, and it borrows that installation's standard library too. What the environment owns is its own site packages folder, where every package this project installs will go, and nowhere else. sys dot prefix points into the project, while sys dot base prefix still points at the installation it was made from. That is the whole point: two projects on one machine can need different packages, or different versions of the same package, and each keeps its own. The folder even writes its own git ignore file, so it never ends up in version control. With a Python of its own, the project is ready for its first file.

The pipeline begins as a single file, main dot py. It is nothing more than text, four lines of it, and the explorer marks it as new. The first line starts with a hash sign, which makes it a comment: a note for people, which Python skips entirely. The second line is blank. The two lines after that are the first real code in the project, and both of them call print. In the terminal, python main dot py hands the file to the interpreter from our environment. Python reads it from the top to the bottom and runs each line in order, which is why the table on the right walks down the file one line at a time. The comment and the blank line do nothing. Line three prints the pipeline's banner. Line four prints a price. Look at how that line is built, because the second table on the right takes it apart. print was given three separate things, separated by commas: some text, a number, and some more text. Text in quotes is called a string, and a number with a decimal point is called a float. print turns each of them into characters, puts a single space between them, and ends the line, so three arguments become one line in the terminal. Notice that the quotes never appear in the output: they only tell Python where the text starts and ends. This is the shape every program in the course will have. A file of instructions, an interpreter that runs them in order, and output you can read. Next, before we write the next line, we will try it out first, in the REPL.

Python has a second way to run code, and it is the one you will reach for whenever you are not sure what a line will do. Typing python on its own, here with dash q to skip the banner, opens the REPL. The name describes the loop on the right: it reads the line you type, evaluates it, prints the value, and waits for the next one. Unlike a script, it shows you the value of everything, without being asked. We want main dot py to print what three bags of coffee cost, so we try it here first. nine point nine five comes straight back. Three bags, nine point nine five times three, comes back as twenty nine point eight four nine nine nine, and a long tail of nines. That is not a typing mistake, and it is not a bug in Python. A float stores numbers in binary, and nine point nine five has no exact binary form, so what you get is the nearest value a float can hold. The REPL is also good for small questions about text: the first three characters of the product code come back as E T H. Then exit leaves the REPL, and everything typed there is gone; the table at the bottom puts the REPL and the file side by side. Trying the line has done its job, so we write it into main dot py as line five and run the file. The new line prints the same long number. For a coffee shop, that is the wrong answer: money must come out in exact cents. We will leave it here for now, deliberately, and fix it properly in the next course, with a type made for money.

Every programmer breaks their code many times a day, so the most useful skill in this course may be reading what Python says when it happens. Here line five has lost its closing bracket. We run the file, and look closely at the terminal: there is no banner. Line three is perfectly correct, yet it never printed. That tells you when this error was found. Before Python runs a single line, its parser reads the whole file and checks its grammar: every bracket closed, every colon in place. The diagram on the right follows that path. The parser reached the end of the file with a bracket still open, so it stopped, and nothing ran at all. Now read the error itself, line by line, with the table beside it. The first line names the file and the line number, five. The second line shows that line of code. The third line has a caret pointing up, at the bracket that was opened and never closed. And the last line says what kind of error this is, a SyntaxError, followed by a plain description: the opening bracket was never closed. Python's messages have become far more helpful in recent versions, and this one says exactly what is wrong. Notice that the caret points at where the bracket was opened, not at where the missing one belongs. For a missing bracket, the true mistake is often at the end of the line, or even on a later line. So the habit is to read the last line of the error first, then the line it points at, then look around it. Next, an error that the parser cannot see.

This time every bracket is in place, but on line four, print has been typed as p r n t. As far as the parser is concerned, that is perfectly good Python: p r n t is a valid name, so the file passes the grammar check and starts running. The table on the right shows what happened, line by line. Line three runs, and the banner appears in the terminal. Then line four runs, and Python has to find out what p r n t means. It looks in two places, shown in the diagram: the names this file has defined, and then the built in names that every program starts with, such as print and len. Neither has anything called p r n t, so Python raises a NameError, and line five never runs. The traceback reads the same way as before. It gives the file and the line, underlines the name it could not find, and on the last line names the error and adds a suggestion: did you mean print? Python suggests a close match whenever it can find one, and it is usually right. The table at the bottom is the real lesson of this pair. A SyntaxError is found by the parser, before any line runs, so nothing happens at all. A NameError is found by the running program, only when it reaches the bad line, so everything before that line has already happened. Here that means one printed banner. In a pipeline that writes files, it could mean half a report already written, which is why this course will test its code, and check its input before it writes anything. Fix the name, and the project is set up. In the next course, it starts to hold real data.

Course two ended with a misspelt name. The first change in this course fixes it, and then starts holding the data our pipeline is about: one line of one order. main dot py now gives three things names. sku is the product code, a piece of text. price is nine point nine five, and quantity is three. The last line prints all three with the line's total, and the terminal shows the familiar long number, which we fix in the next section. The table at the bottom of the right hand pane lists those names, what each refers to, and the type of that object: a string, a float and an integer. You met the key idea in course one: a name refers to an object, and assignment binds a name; it never copies. The REPL makes it concrete. We set quantity to three, then write bags equals quantity. The top diagram shows the result: two names, one object, the integer three. Then quantity equals quantity plus one. Python evaluates the right hand side first, making a new integer, four, and then moves the name quantity to it. The second diagram shows what changed: only quantity's arrow moved. bags still refers to the three, and asking for both confirms it: four, and three. Integers cannot be changed in place; arithmetic always produces a new object, and the name is simply moved to point at it. This is why reassigning one name never affects another, and it is the first half of a lesson that pays off at the end of this course, when the objects can be changed. Next, why the price is the wrong kind of number.

Python has more than one kind of number, and the pipeline has to pick the right one for money. In the REPL, zero point one plus zero point two gives zero point three, followed by a long run of zeros and a four. That is not a Python bug; every language that uses binary floating point gives the same answer, because zero point one has no exact binary form, just like a third has no exact decimal form. For measurements that is fine. For money it is not: an invoice cannot be wrong by a fraction of a cent, and small errors grow when you add thousands of them. The standard library's answer is the decimal module. A Decimal stores decimal digits exactly, so Decimal of zero point one plus Decimal of zero point two is exactly zero point three. There is one trap, and the REPL shows it. Decimal of nine point nine five, written without quotes, is built from a float, and the float's error comes with it, kept exactly, all fifty digits of it. The diagram in the middle of the pane draws the rule: make a Decimal from text, never from a float. The text nine point nine five, exactly as the shop wrote it, becomes exactly nine point nine five. So main dot py now imports Decimal, the price is created from a string, and the terminal shows three bags costing twenty nine point eight five, to the cent. The table at the bottom sums up the three kinds of number this course uses: integers for quantities, floats for measurements, and Decimal for every amount of money, from here to the end. Next, the product code, which is text.

Our product codes carry information. E T H dash two fifty means Ethiopian coffee in a two hundred and fifty gram bag, and the pipeline will need both halves. A string is a sequence of characters, and the table at the top of the right hand pane lays out the seven characters of this one, with their positions. Positions start at zero, so the E is at index zero. They can also be counted from the end, using negative numbers, so the final zero is at index minus one. Slicing takes a run of characters: a start, a colon, and an end, where the end itself is not included. So sku, from the start up to three, is E T H, and sku from four onwards is the digits, two five zero. In the REPL, the last three characters, minus three onwards, give the same digits. The split method breaks a string wherever it finds the separator you give it, and returns a list of the pieces, one for the origin and one for the size. Notice the quotes in the answers. Two five zero, sliced out of a string, is still a string, text that looks like a number. Python will not do arithmetic with it, and will not guess. The diagram below the tables makes that conversion explicit: the int function turns the text into the integer two hundred and fifty. main dot py now does exactly that, and the terminal prints the product's origin and its weight in grams. One more thing to know: strings cannot be changed. Every slice, and every method that seems to modify one, returns a new string. Next, values that answer yes or no, and values that might be missing.

Some values answer a question, and some values are missing, and the pipeline has to handle both without confusing them. A comparison produces a boolean, one of two values, True or False. main dot py asks whether the quantity is ten or more, the shop's rule for a wholesale order. Three is not, so the comparison gives False, and the diagram at the top shows the name is wholesale keeping that answer. The discount code is a different problem, because it might not exist. Python's built in way to say there is no value is None. Our first line's customer used no code, so discount code is None, and the terminal prints it. The table in the middle shows why this needs care. A code can be a string, a real code that was entered. It can be None, meaning the customer had no code. And sometimes there is a third state: nobody told us at all, because the field was not in the data. If you use None for that as well, the two meanings collide. Python three point fifteen adds a tool for exactly this, the sentinel. In the REPL, we create one called NOT GIVEN. It is a unique object with a name, and it is not None. And here is a subtlety the REPL exposes: None counts as false, but the sentinel counts as true. That is why you should test for these values by identity, with is None or is NOT GIVEN, rather than by truthiness, because an empty string and zero are false too, and they are perfectly good values. The table at the bottom summarises the sentinel. We will use one in course five, when rows arrive with fields missing. Next, many order lines at once.

One order line is not a day of business. The shop's first day has four lines, and Python's everyday way to hold several values in order is a list. main dot py now has two lists: the product codes of the four lines, and their quantities. The diagram on the right draws each one as a list object, with numbered slots starting at zero, and a name referring to each. Two of the slots in the codes list hold the same product, Ethiopian, because two customers ordered it, and a list is perfectly happy to hold duplicates. Lists come with useful tools, and the table below shows four of them. len gives the number of items, four lines. sum adds up numbers, so the quantities total eighteen bags, and the terminal shows both. An index in square brackets picks out one item, so skus at zero is the first code. And a list can change: in the REPL, append adds a new item at the end, and the list grows from two codes to three. That ability to change is what makes lists the right home for a day's orders, which arrive one at a time. The same section shows a weakness in this design, and the note at the bottom names it. The two lists only belong together by position. The quantity for the third code is whatever sits in slot two of the other list. Add a line to one list and forget the other, and every line after it is silently wrong. That kind of mistake does not raise an error, which makes it dangerous. The fix is to keep each line's values together as one record. Next, the tuple.

An order line is a record: an order number, a product code and a quantity that belong together. Python's simplest record is a tuple, written with round brackets, and main dot py now holds the day as a list of four tuples, one per line. The two parallel lists are gone, and with them the risk of the values drifting apart. A tuple is like a list in that it keeps its items in order and you can index it. The difference is that a tuple cannot be changed. In the REPL, trying to set the quantity of the first line to four fails with a TypeError: a tuple does not support item assignment. The table in the middle of the pane puts the two side by side. A list holds many things of one kind and can grow, like the day's lines. A tuple holds one fixed record, like a single line. That fixedness is a feature: a record that cannot change by accident is one less thing to worry about. Tuples also make unpacking natural, and main dot py uses it on line fifteen. order id, sku, quantity equals the first line. Python takes the tuple's three slots and binds three names, one each, from left to right, which is exactly what the diagram at the top draws. The number of names has to match the number of slots, or Python raises an error rather than guessing. The output shows the first line, priced, and the total is still correct to the cent. But look at the price on line sixteen: it is still a single value written by hand, the same for every product. To price every line, the pipeline needs a way to look prices up. Next, the dictionary.

A dictionary maps keys to values, and it solves two problems at once. First, the catalogue. main dot py now defines CATALOGUE, a dictionary from each product code to its price, written in capitals because it is a constant the program should not change. Second, the order lines themselves. Each line is now a dictionary too, with named fields: id, customer, sku and quantity. That is clearer than a tuple, where you had to remember that the quantity lived in slot two. The customer field is new, and we will need it. The diagram at the top shows the two dictionaries working together, for the first line. Its sku field holds E T H two fifty, and using that as a key in the catalogue looks up the price, nine point nine five, which is what line twenty two does. The terminal confirms the first line still comes to twenty nine point eight five. In the REPL, asking the catalogue for Colombian returns its price as a Decimal. Asking for B R A five hundred, a Brazilian coffee that is not in our catalogue yet, raises a KeyError, naming the key it could not find. That is the correct behaviour: a pipeline that quietly priced an unknown product at zero would be far worse. We will handle unknown products properly in course four. The table at the bottom explains why dictionaries are fast. Python computes a hash of the key, a number derived from it, and that number tells it where to look. So looking up a key takes one step, whether the dictionary holds three products or three million. Next, a collection with no duplicates, and a dictionary that cannot change.

Two more collections round out what the pipeline needs to hold. The first is the set. A set holds each value at most once, and it has no order. In the REPL, a set written with four customer names, Maya twice, has a length of three: the duplicate simply disappears. The diagram at the top shows four names going in and three coming out. That makes sets the natural answer to questions like how many different customers ordered today, which our report will ask in course six. Sets have a second strength, shown in the middle table: checking whether something is in them. To check membership in a list, Python compares each item in turn, so the time grows with the length of the list. A set uses hashing, like a dictionary, so it looks in one place, and the check takes about the same time however large the set grows. Course eleven measures that difference. The second change is to the catalogue. Our prices are a constant: nothing in the pipeline should ever change one while it runs. Until now, that was only a convention, signalled by capital letters. Python three point fifteen adds frozendict, a dictionary that cannot be changed after it is created. main dot py now wraps the catalogue in it. Everything that reads a dictionary works exactly as before, as the terminal shows. But in the REPL, trying to set a price raises a TypeError: a frozendict does not support item assignment. A rule that was only a convention is now enforced by Python itself, which is the safest kind of rule. Next, structures inside structures, and what copying really copies.

Real data nests: lists of dictionaries, dictionaries of lists. main dot py now keeps the day's orders under its date, in a dictionary called DAYS, ready for the month of files we will read in course five. But there is a question hiding in that line, and it is the most important idea in this course: does DAYS hold a copy of the orders, or the orders themselves? Remember course one: a container stores references to objects, not copies of them. So DAYS at the first of October refers to the very same list as ORDERS. The REPL proves it, and shows what copying really does. First we make two copies of the order list. copy dot copy makes a shallow copy: a new list, whose slots refer to the same order dictionaries. copy dot deepcopy makes a deep copy: a new list, and new dictionaries inside it, all the way down. Then we change the first order's quantity to four, through ORDERS. Look at the answers. Through DAYS, the quantity is four, because DAYS holds the same list. Through the shallow copy, it is also four. The list is new, but its first slot still refers to the same dictionary we just changed. That is the top diagram. Only the deep copy still says three, because it has its own dictionaries, as the second diagram shows. This is behind a whole family of bugs, where data changes somewhere the code never touched it. The rule of thumb is to change data in one clearly owned place, and copy deliberately when you need independence. That completes holding the data: numbers, text, missing values, and four kinds of collection. In the next course, we start processing it.

Holding data is half the job; this course processes it, and processing starts with expressions. An expression is anything Python can evaluate to a value, and the order it evaluates the parts in matters. In the REPL, two plus three times four is fourteen, not twenty, because multiplication binds more tightly than addition. Brackets change the order, so two plus three, in brackets, times four, is twenty. Three more operators complete the arithmetic we need. Double slash is floor division, so seven divided this way by two is three. Percent gives the remainder, which is one. And double star raises to a power, so two to the power three is eight. The table on the right collects those answers. main dot py now computes something real: the second order line, twelve bags of Colombian. Its subtotal is the price times the quantity, two hundred and ten. Then the line at the bottom of the editor applies a fifteen percent discount: the subtotal, minus the subtotal times nought point one five. The tree at the top of the pane draws how Python reads that. Because multiplication binds more tightly, the right hand multiplication happens first, giving thirty one and a half, and only then is it subtracted from two hundred and ten. No brackets are needed, though you may add them whenever a reader might doubt the order. The result is then rounded to whole cents with quantize, using a constant called CENT, a Decimal of one hundredth, now defined at the top of the file. The terminal shows the line coming to one hundred seventy eight fifty. Fifteen percent is not always right, though. Next, the program decides.

The shop has two discount rules, and they are the pipeline's first real decision. Ten or more bags of one coffee is a wholesale line, and gets fifteen percent off. Otherwise, a line worth fifty or more gets five percent. Anything else pays full price. In Python, decisions are written with if, elif, which is short for else if, and else. Each condition is checked in order, the first one that is true has its block run, and the rest are skipped. Look at the indentation in the editor: the lines that belong to a branch are indented under it, and that indentation is not decoration. Python uses it to decide which lines are inside which block. The chart on the right draws the same rules. For our line of twelve bags, the first question is already true, so the rate is fifteen percent, and the second question is never even asked. That path is lit. The order of the branches is part of the rule. If the fifty check came first, twelve bags of Colombian, worth two hundred and ten, would get only five percent. The table below the chart applies the rules to every line of the first day. Three bags worth twenty nine eighty five get nothing, two bags of Kenyan worth sixty two get five percent, and so on. Python also has a one line form for choosing between two values, the conditional expression. In the REPL, the word wholesale if quantity is ten or more, else retail, gives wholesale. Use it for short choices like this one; anything longer reads better as a full if statement. Next, a decision based not on a value, but on a shape.

Real data is messy, and the first messy line has arrived. The shop's system sent a fifth order, O R D ten oh five, whose quantity is not a number but the word three, typed into the field by hand. Before the pipeline can price a line, it has to ask what shape the line is, and Python's match statement is built for exactly that question. match takes a value and compares it against a series of patterns, in order, until one fits. The first pattern here describes a good line: a dictionary with a sku and a quantity, where the quantity is an integer, followed by a guard, if quantity is greater than zero. When a pattern matches, it also binds names to the parts it found, so sku and quantity are ready to use inside that case. The second pattern only asks for a quantity, of any kind. The diagram on the right follows our bad line through the cases. The first pattern fails, because the text three is a string, not an integer. Python moves on to the second case, which matches, and binds the name qty to the word three, so the program can say exactly what was wrong. The terminal shows it: cannot price O R D ten oh five, quantity three. The table at the bottom shows how to read the pieces of a pattern. Curly braces match a dictionary with those keys, int in a pattern checks the type, and if adds an extra condition. And case underscore, which we will use soon, matches anything at all. Notice what did not happen here: no crash, and no wrong price. So far, though, we have only checked one line. Next, every line of the day.

Pricing one line by hand does not make a pipeline. A for loop runs the same block of code once for each item in a collection, and main dot py now uses one to price every line of the day. The loop's first line says: for each line in ORDERS. On every pass, Python binds the name line to the next dictionary in the list, and runs the indented block below. The diagram on the right freezes the loop on its second pass: the name line now refers to O R D ten oh two, and the running total holds the first line's twenty nine eighty five. Inside the loop, the match statement from the last section decides what to do with each line. A good line gets priced, using the same discount rules as before, now indented one level deeper because they belong to the loop. Its total is added to the day's total with plus equals, which is short for adding to the name and binding it again. Anything else falls through to case underscore, which matches any line at all, and prints that it was skipped. The terminal, and the table below the diagram, show the result. Four lines priced, each with its own discount: twenty nine eighty five, one hundred seventy eight fifty, fifty eight ninety and nine ninety five. The bad line is skipped, with its reason. And after the loop finishes, the day's total: two hundred seventy seven twenty, to the cent. Notice the last line of the file is not indented: it runs once, after the loop. That is the whole of a loop: indentation decides what repeats. The loop works, but the pricing is nested deep inside a case. Next, flatter loops, and two ways to leave one.

Deeply nested code is hard to read, and the loop from the last section has the important work buried three levels deep. Two small keywords fix that. The match now only checks the line. If the line is bad, the case adds one to a skipped counter and says continue, which ends this pass immediately and moves on to the next line. A good line falls through to the pricing, which now sits at the loop's own level. The terminal shows the same four totals and the same day total as before, and now a count of one skipped line. The bottom of the file adds something the report will want: the first wholesale order of the day. It uses Python's other loop, while, which repeats for as long as a condition stays true. Here the condition is that the index i is still inside the list. The table at the top of the right hand pane steps through it. At index zero, the first line has three bags, not wholesale, so i goes up by one. At index one, the second line has twelve bags. That is a wholesale order, so the program prints it, and then says break, which leaves the loop entirely, without checking the remaining lines. The middle of the pane puts the two exits side by side: continue skips to the next pass, break leaves the loop. So when should you use which loop? A for loop runs once per item, and is almost always the right choice for walking through a list or a file. A while loop is for when you control the step yourself, and it has a famous trap: if nothing inside it changes its condition, it never ends. Next, loops written in a single line.

Some loops exist only to build a collection, and Python has a compact form for those: the comprehension. The orders now span two days. DAYS holds the first of October's list and a second day with one more line, and the pipeline should process them all. The first comprehension, the highlighted line under the data, flattens them into a single list. It reads: star day, for each day in the values of DAYS. The star unpacks each day's list into the new one, so two lists become one list of six lines. Unpacking inside a comprehension is new in Python three point fifteen, and the diagram at the top of the pane draws it. The loop now collects each priced line, with its total, into a list called priced. After the loop, three more comprehensions summarise it, each in one line. The bags are the sum of each line's quantity. The customers are a set, written with curly braces, of each line's customer, so the duplicate Maya disappears, and sorted turns the set into a list in alphabetical order. The table in the middle of the pane shows how to read one. It is a loop written backwards: what to keep comes first, then the for that produces it. The terminal shows the result of all that: a total of two hundred ninety four seventy across the two days, nineteen bags, one skipped line, and three customers. Comprehensions are at their best when they say one simple thing. If you find yourself writing conditions inside conditions, or a comprehension that does several jobs, write the loop instead: it will be easier to read. Next, the pricing becomes a piece we can name.

The pricing rules now sit in the middle of a loop, where nothing else can use them and nobody can test them on their own. A function fixes both problems: it gives a step a name. main dot py now defines two. discount rate takes a quantity and a subtotal, and returns the rate, with the same rules as before, written as returns. The docstring under its first line says what it does, in plain words. price line takes a product and a quantity, computes the subtotal, asks discount rate for the rate, and returns the line's total, rounded to the cent. The loop has shrunk to a single call: total equals price line of sku and quantity. The output has not changed at all, which is exactly what a good refactoring should look like. What changed is the shape. Each call creates a frame, as you saw in course one. The diagram on the right freezes the stack while discount rate is running for the twelve bag line. Its frame is on top, with its own quantity and subtotal. Under it, price line's frame is paused, waiting, and under that, the module's loop. When discount rate returns nought point one five, its frame is popped, and price line carries on; when price line returns one hundred seventy eight fifty, the loop carries on. And now the pricing can be tried on its own. In the REPL, after the script has run, calling price line with Colombian and twelve gives one hundred seventy eight fifty, without touching the orders at all. Testing a function by calling it directly is the seed of course ten. Next, the ways values get into a function.

A function is only as useful as the ways you can call it. price line now takes a third parameter, catalogue, with a default value: CATALOGUE. A call that leaves it out gets the shop's real prices, exactly as before. A call that passes a different catalogue, for example a test with made up prices, gets those instead, and the function body now uses whichever catalogue it was given. The table in the middle of the right hand pane shows the three ways arguments arrive. By position, matched in order. By keyword, where you name the parameter, which makes long calls far easier to read. And by default, when the caller leaves it out. Defaults have one famous trap, and the REPL walks straight into it. add reason takes a reason, and a list to add it to, which defaults to an empty list. Call it once with bad quantity, and you get a list holding bad quantity. Call it again with unknown product, and you would expect a fresh list holding just that. Instead you get both reasons. The diagram at the top shows why. A default value is created once, when the def statement runs, and stored on the function. Every call that relies on the default receives that same list, so each call adds to what the previous ones left behind. For numbers and strings, which cannot change, that never matters. For a list or a dictionary, it causes bugs that appear only on the second call. The fix, shown at the bottom, is to default to None and create a new list inside the function. Our catalogue default is safe, because a frozendict can never change. Next, where Python looks names up.

Rounding to the cent appears in more than one place, so main dot py gives it a function of its own: to cents, which quantizes an amount using CENT. price line now calls it. The output is unchanged. But look at what to cents does: it uses CENT without being given it. So where does that name come from? Python looks names up in a fixed order, often called L E G B, and the diagram on the right walks through it for CENT. First, the local scope: the names created inside this call of to cents, which is just its parameter, amount. No CENT there. Next, any enclosing function: to cents is not inside another function, so there is none. Next, the global scope: the names defined at the top level of main dot py. CENT is found there, and the search stops. Only if it had failed there would Python look in the built ins, the names like print and sum that every program starts with, and only after that would it raise a NameError. Reading a name searches outwards like this. Assigning a name is different, and the REPL shows how. We set rate to the word global. Then we define a function, show, which assigns rate to the word local and returns it. Calling it, and then asking for rate, gives local, and global. The assignment inside the function created a new, local name, and left the global one alone. That is deliberate: a function cannot accidentally overwrite the names around it. Python does have keywords to rebind an outer name, global and nonlocal, but needing them is usually a sign the code should pass values in and return them instead. Next, what happens when something goes wrong.

A new line has arrived that the pipeline cannot price: two bags of B R A five hundred, a Brazilian coffee the shop has just started selling, which is not in our catalogue yet. You saw in course three what looking up a missing key does: it raises a KeyError. Without any help, that error would stop the whole run at this line, and none of the later lines would be priced. The diagram on the right follows the error. It is raised inside price line, when the catalogue lookup fails. price line stops immediately: it never reaches its return, and its frame is removed. The error then travels up to whoever called it, looking for code willing to handle it. That code is the try statement now wrapped around the call in the loop. try says: run this, and if one of these errors happens, run the except block instead. Our except block names the error it expects, KeyError. It prints that the line was skipped, and why, counts it, and continues with the next line. The terminal shows the result in the table below the diagram. The run reaches the end. O R D ten oh six is skipped as an unknown product, the line from the second day is still priced, and the total is the same as before, with two lines skipped. Two habits matter here. Catch only the errors you expect, and catch them where you can actually decide what to do about them. A bare except that swallows every error would also hide a typo in your own code. This version works, but it is still vague: a KeyError could come from anywhere. Next, an error the pipeline owns.

The pipeline now rejects lines for two different reasons, in two different places: a bad quantity in the loop, and an unknown product inside price line. The last step of this course brings both together, under an error of our own. A new class, InvalidOrder, is defined near the top of the file. It inherits from Exception, Python's base class for errors, and its docstring says what it means: a line the pipeline refuses to price, and why. We will look at classes properly in course nine; for now, two lines are all an exception class needs. price line now does its own checking. The match statement has moved inside it, and when the quantity is wrong, it raises InvalidOrder, with a message naming the line and the bad value. When the product is unknown, it raises InvalidOrder again, naming the product, instead of letting a KeyError escape. The loop is now simple. It tries to price each line. If that raises InvalidOrder, it keeps the error in a list called rejected and moves on. The diagram on the right shows the two ways out of price line. At the end, the program prints the total, the number of rejected lines, and then every rejection with its reason, as the table shows: the quantity three, and the unknown product B R A five hundred. This is the principle the whole pipeline will follow. A clear error is better than a wrong answer, and the run must never stop silently, or carry on silently either. Every line is either priced or reported. That completes processing the data. In the next course, the orders stop being typed into the program, and are read from real files.

Until now, the orders were typed into the program. Real orders come from the shop, as one file per day, and this course is about reading them. The explorer shows a new folder, data slash raw, holding the first day's file, a CSV: a header line naming the columns, and one line per order. main dot py now opens it. The key line starts with the word with: with open the file, as file. Inside that block, the program reads the first line, the header, splits it at the commas, and then loops over the remaining lines, pairing each line's values with the header's names. The diagram in the middle of the right hand pane shows that pairing for the first order: zip puts the five column names beside the five values, and dict turns the pairs into the same kind of dictionary we used before. Why with? A file you open must be closed, or the operating system keeps it open, and on a busy machine that eventually fails. The with statement closes it for you when the block ends, and the diagram at the top shows the important part: it closes it even if an error happens inside the block. In the REPL, after the script has run, file dot closed is True. Notice one more thing in the editor. Everything read from a file is text. The quantity three arrives as the string three, so the program converts quantities made of digits into integers before pricing. The word three stays text, and is still rejected. The terminal shows the same totals as at the end of the last course, which is exactly the point: the data moved into a file, and the answers did not change. Next, a file that is not quite what it seems.

The second day's file comes from the shop's old till, and it hides a problem you cannot see by looking at it. A file is not text; it is bytes, and turning bytes into text needs an encoding, a rule for which bytes mean which characters. The modern standard is UTF eight, and Python three point fifteen now uses it by default whenever you open a file. The old till, though, saves files in an older encoding called Latin one. For plain letters and digits the two agree. They disagree as soon as a customer has an accent. The table at the top of the pane shows the name Zoé as the till saved it: two ordinary bytes, then one byte for the é. In Latin one, that byte means é. In UTF eight, a byte like that cannot appear on its own, so decoding it as UTF eight fails. main dot py now reads both day files through a new function, read text. It asks for UTF eight first. If that raises a UnicodeDecodeError, it says so on the terminal, and reads the file as Latin one instead, because the shop has confirmed that is what the old till writes. The second command, file, is a standard tool that guesses a file's type, and it agrees: ISO eight eight five nine, which is Latin one's official name. Now the second day prices correctly, including Zoé's two bags. Two habits matter. Always say which encoding you mean, even though three point fifteen now defaults to UTF eight; and never let a program guess silently. Ours guesses only from a short list the shop confirmed, and it tells you every time it does. Next, finding every day's file automatically.

Naming each day's file by hand will not survive a month. The pathlib module represents file system paths as objects, and main dot py now uses one: RAW, a Path for the data slash raw folder. Its glob method finds every file whose name matches a pattern, here orders dash star dot csv, and sorted puts them in date order. The diagram at the top shows the three files it found, including a new third day. Paths come apart into useful pieces, and the REPL shows them for the first file: the full name, the stem, which is the name without its extension, and the suffix, dot csv. DAYS is now built from whatever files exist, using each file's stem, minus the word orders, as the date. A fourth file tomorrow will simply appear in the report. The read text function now uses the path's own read text method, and the run prints a total for each day instead of every line. But look closely at the output, in the table at the bottom of the pane. There is a new rejection: order ten twelve, with a quantity of B R A five hundred. That is not bad data from the shop. That is a bug in our program. The third day includes a customer recorded as smith, comma, kim, and because the name contains a comma, the CSV file puts it in quotes. Our code splits each line at every comma, so the name was cut in two, every value after it shifted one column to the right, and the product code landed in the quantity column. Validation caught it, which is good. But the fix belongs in the reading, not the checking. Next, a proper CSV reader.

CSV looks simple enough to parse by hand, and the last section showed why you should not. The format has rules: a value containing a comma is wrapped in double quotes, a quote inside a value is doubled, and a value can even contain a line break. Python's csv module knows all of them, and main dot py now uses its DictReader. read day hands it the file's lines, and DictReader does what our zip loop did, turning each row into a dictionary keyed by the header, except that it does it correctly. The diagram at the top of the right hand pane puts the two side by side, for order ten twelve. Splitting at every comma gives six pieces, with the customer's name broken across two of them. The csv reader gives five fields, with the customer exactly as written: smith, comma, kim. In the REPL, the last row of the third day confirms it. With the reading fixed, the run tells the truth about order ten twelve. It is still rejected, but now for its real reason: four bags of B R A five hundred, a product our catalogue does not have. The Brazilian coffee has come up twice now, and both times the problem is the same. The shop has started selling it, and our catalogue, still typed into main dot py, has not caught up. Every time a price changes or a product is added, someone has to edit the program. That is a sign the catalogue does not belong in the code at all. It is data, and data lives in files. Next, the catalogue moves into a file of its own.

The shop keeps its product list in a file called catalogue dot json, which now sits beside the order files, and it includes the Brazilian coffee at sixteen twenty five. JSON is the most common format for structured data passed between programs: objects in curly braces, lists in square brackets, strings, numbers, true, false and null. Python's json module turns it into the types you know, and the diagram at the top of the pane shows the mapping. A JSON object becomes a dictionary, a string becomes a str, and a number becomes an int or, if it has a decimal point, a float. That last mapping is why the shop's file writes every price as a string. A float would bring back the binary rounding errors from course three. As a string, nine point nine five arrives exactly, and main dot py's new read catalogue function turns each one into a Decimal and freezes the result, just as before. The table in the middle shows the catalogue as it was read. The constant typed into the program is gone. In the REPL, the Brazilian coffee is now there, at sixteen twenty five, as a Decimal. And the run shows the effect: both Brazilian lines, order ten oh six on the first day and order ten twelve on the third, are priced, and only one line is still rejected, the quantity three. The day totals have changed to match. Nothing in the pricing code had to change for this. That is what separating data from code buys you: the next time the shop adds a coffee or changes a price, it edits a file, and the program is untouched. Next, the shop's mistakes multiply, and the pipeline needs a proper gate.

Real files contain real mistakes, and the shop has sent three more on the third day: a line with no customer, a quantity of minus one, and a short line that stops before its quantity. Until now, the only checks lived in price line, mixed in with the pricing. main dot py now separates the two jobs. A new function, parse row, takes a raw CSV row, where every value is still text, and either returns a clean order line, with its quantity converted to an integer, or raises InvalidOrder saying exactly what is wrong. price line goes back to doing one thing: pricing a line it can trust. The table at the top of the right hand pane shows parse row's verdict on every row of the third day. The four good rows pass. Order ten thirteen has no customer. Order ten fourteen's quantity, minus one, is not a whole number above zero. And order ten fifteen is short, so its quantity is missing entirely. Notice how parse row tells two kinds of missing apart, using the sentinel from course three, called MISSING. Asking a row for a field that its file has no column for returns MISSING, which means the whole file is wrong. A row that simply left the field empty gives None or an empty string. The table at the bottom shows the difference. The terminal shows the result: four rejections, each with its reason, and every good row still priced. This is the pipeline's contract from now on. Every row that comes in is either priced or reported, and nothing is ever dropped silently. Next, the whole month of files, and a way to read it without holding it all at once.

The shop has now sent the whole of October: thirty one files. Building a dictionary of every day's rows before pricing any of them works for a month, but the same code would need memory for a year, or ten, all at once. A generator avoids that. main dot py replaces read day with iter rows, a function that contains the keyword yield. Calling a function like that does not run it. It returns a generator, an object that produces values one at a time, on request. Each time the loop asks for the next row, iter rows runs until it reaches a yield, hands that row over, and pauses right there, with all of its local variables intact, until it is asked again. Here, yield from passes along every row the csv reader produces, file by file. The diagram at the top of the pane freezes that pause. The REPL makes it concrete: calling iter rows gives us rows, and asking for next of rows twice gives the first two orders of the month, ten oh one and ten oh two. Nothing else has been read yet. The main loop now prices rows as they stream past, keeping only running totals: thirty one files, one hundred sixty three lines priced, thirteen rejected, and an October total of eleven thousand, five hundred seventy eight, and eighty eight cents. The table at the bottom compares the two approaches: a list holds every row before the first is used, while the generator holds one file at a time and hands out one row at a time. That completes reading the data. In the next course, we stop just adding it up, and start asking it questions.

The pipeline can now read a whole month, but so far it only adds everything into one number. The shop's real questions are more specific, and the first is: which coffees earn the money? Answering it means grouping: sorting the priced lines into buckets, one per product, and keeping a running total in each. A dictionary is the natural bucket store, with the product code as the key and its revenue so far as the value. main dot py's loop now does that in two lines. It takes the line's product, then sets that product's revenue to whatever it was before, plus this line's total. The tricky part is the very first line for each product, when there is no entry yet. The get method handles it: revenue dot get of a key, with a default, returns the value if the key exists, and the default otherwise. So the first Brazilian line adds to zero, and every later one adds to the running total. The REPL shows the default in action: asking for Guatemalan, which never appears among the priced lines, returns a Decimal zero rather than raising a KeyError. The diagram on the right shows the idea, every priced line dropping into its product's bucket, and the table holds October's answer. Kenyan coffee earns the most, four thousand four hundred sixty, then Colombian, Ethiopian and Brazilian. The terminal also reports thirteen rejected rows, the same as at the end of the last course, which is a useful sanity check: grouping must not change what counts as valid. One pass over the month, one running total per key: that pattern will answer most of the questions in this course. Next, two tools that make it even shorter.

Grouping is so common that the standard library's collections module has two tools built for it. A defaultdict is a dictionary that creates a missing key the moment you touch it, using a function you give it. revenue is now a defaultdict of Decimal. Calling Decimal with no arguments gives zero, so the first time a product appears, its entry springs into existence at zero, and plus equals simply adds to it. The get call is gone. The diagram at the top of the pane shows that first touch for the Brazilian coffee, on order ten oh six: the key did not exist, it is created at zero, and thirty two fifty is added. A Counter is a dictionary built for counting, where missing keys also start at zero. main dot py now uses two. bags counts how many bags of each product were sold, by adding each line's quantity, and customers counts how many order lines each customer placed, by adding one. Counters come with useful methods of their own, and most common is the one the shop wants: the best customers. The terminal shows revenue and bags side by side for each product, in the table in the middle of the pane, and then the top three customers: Maya and Ana with twenty three lines each, and Lena with twenty two. When two counts are equal, most common keeps them in the order they were first seen, so the answer is the same on every run. Look at the bags column. Ethiopian sells the most bags by far, two hundred and sixty four, but it earns less than Kenyan or Colombian. Which product is top depends entirely on what you rank by. Next, ranking.

A report should lead with what matters, so the products should be listed by revenue, highest first. The built in sorted function returns a new list in order, and its key argument decides what the ordering is based on. The table in the middle of the pane takes main dot py's sorting line apart. revenue dot items gives pairs: a product and its amount. The key is a lambda, a small function written in one line without a name, which receives one pair and returns its second item, the amount. So the pairs are compared by amount, and reverse equals True puts the largest first. Then enumerate numbers the ranked pairs as the loop goes, starting at one instead of the default zero, and each pair is unpacked straight into a product and an amount. The terminal, and the chart at the top of the pane, show the ranking: Kenyan, Colombian, Ethiopian, Brazilian. Notice that sorted never changes the dictionary itself. It reads the items, and builds a new list, which is the safest kind of operation. The key does not have to be a lambda. Any function that takes one item will do. In the REPL, sorting the products by bags passes the Counter's own get method as the key, so each product is compared by its bag count, and the answer comes back in the opposite order, smallest first: Brazilian, Kenyan, Colombian, Ethiopian. The note at the bottom says why the two rankings differ: Kenyan sells few bags, but each one is a kilogram at thirty one. Rank by the question you are actually asking. Next, the middle of the numbers, and when to round.

The shop wants to know what a typical order line is worth, and how much coffee to roast each day. The statistics module answers the first question. main dot py now keeps every line's total in a list, and the terminal reports three numbers: the mean, seventy one oh four, the median, forty nine seventy five, and the largest line, three hundred sixteen twenty. The chart at the top of the pane shows them side by side. Why is the mean so far above the median? The median is the middle value when the lines are sorted, so half the lines are worth less and half are worth more. The mean is the total divided by the count, and a handful of large wholesale lines pull it upwards. When a few big values dominate, the median is the better answer to what is typical, and a good report gives both. Notice that the mean is rounded to cents only when it is printed. Round money at the end, never part way through a calculation, or the small errors add up. The second question needs a decision about rounding. Across October, the shop sold twenty three point four eight bags a day, on average. You cannot roast part of a bag, and running short is worse than having one spare, so the program rounds up, with math dot ceil, to twenty four. The REPL compares the options. ceil always rounds up, floor always rounds down, and the built in round, on a value exactly halfway, rounds to the nearest even number: two point five becomes two, and three point five becomes four. That surprises people, and it is exactly why rounding should always be a deliberate choice. Next, the dates in the data.

Every order line carries its date, but so far only as text. The datetime module turns text into real dates, and real dates can answer questions text cannot. main dot py now converts each line's date with date dot fromisoformat, the standard way to read a date written year, month, day. It adds the line's total to two new groupings: one by date, and one by ISO week number, which isocalendar provides. The terminal then reports the busiest day of the month and the total for each week. The busiest day was Wednesday the seventh of October, with eleven hundred and six eighty one. strftime turned that date into words, using a format string where percent capital A means the weekday name, percent d the day, and percent capital B the month. The table in the middle of the pane shows those steps. In the REPL, the busiest day's isocalendar gives its year, its week number, forty one, and its weekday, three, because ISO weeks count Monday as day one. The chart at the top of the pane shows the five weeks. And the note at the bottom points out a trap that has fooled many real reports. Week forty looks terrible, at seven hundred, and week forty four looks weak too. But October twenty twenty six starts on a Thursday and ends on a Saturday, so week forty only contains four days of the month, and week forty four contains six. Compare only whole weeks, or the chart tells a story the business did not live. Dates have many traps like this, from month lengths to time zones, which is why you should always reach for datetime rather than doing date arithmetic on text. Next, iterating without building lists.

The itertools module is a toolkit for working with iterators, and it fits our streaming pipeline perfectly. main dot py now starts by wrapping the row loop in a generator of its own, priced lines. It takes rows, and a list to put rejections in, and yields each valid line with its total attached, so validation and pricing happen lazily, one row at a time, as before. Then groupby. Given a stream and a key, groupby collects neighbouring items that share the same key into one group. Here the key is each line's date, fetched with itemgetter, a tidy way to say give me this field. Because the day files are read in date order, each day's lines arrive next to each other, and groupby hands them over one day at a time. The note at the bottom is the one rule to remember: groupby only groups neighbours, so its input must already be sorted by the key, or the same day would appear several times. The diagram at the top of the pane shows the whole chain: rows flow into priced lines, into groupby, and only the thirty one daily totals are kept. Nothing in the middle builds a list. Then islice, which takes the first few items of any iterable, like slicing a list, but without needing a list. The terminal uses it to preview the first three days: three hundred nine seventy, thirty seven forty, and two hundred sixty one forty. The REPL shows the third tool, chain, which joins several iterables end to end, so one product list followed by another reads as one list of three. Together these let the pipeline work on a month, or a year, in constant memory. Next, all of this becomes one step.

Over this course, main dot py has grown a collection of loops and counters, each answering one question. The final step gathers them into one function, and that function is the transform stage of the pipeline. summarise takes the priced lines, makes one pass over them, grouping by day, and returns a dictionary holding everything the report needs: revenue ranked by product, bags, customers, daily and weekly totals, the overall total, the mean and the median. Look at what it does not do. It reads no files, prints nothing and touches no names outside its argument. Lines go in, a summary comes out, which is exactly what the diagram on the right draws. In the REPL, sorted of summary lists its keys, from bags to weekly. The bottom of the file is now short: build the priced lines from the files, pass them to summarise, and print a small report. The terminal shows it, and the table on the right repeats it: October's total of eleven thousand five hundred seventy eight eighty eight, thirteen rejected rows, Kenyan coffee as the top product, Maya as the best customer, and the mean and median line. Why does this shape matter? Because each stage of the pipeline can now be understood, changed and checked on its own. The reading part knows nothing about discounts. The summarising part knows nothing about files, which means that in course ten we can test it by handing it three made up lines and checking the answer, without a single file on disk. That is the transform stage done. The pipeline can read the month and answer the shop's questions. In the next course, it writes the answers down.

The pipeline can now answer the shop's questions, but every answer disappears when the program ends. The last stage, load, writes the results somewhere they last. The first output is for people: a daily report the owner can open in a spreadsheet. CSV is the obvious format, and the csv module that read the orders can write them too. main dot py has a new function, write report. It takes the daily totals and a path. First it makes sure the output folder exists: mkdir with parents equals True creates data and out if they are missing, and exist ok equals True means a second run is not an error. Then it opens the file for writing, with newline set to an empty string. That looks odd, but it hands the line endings to the csv module, which writes them correctly on every operating system. csv dot writer wraps the open file, and each call to writerow turns one Python list into one row: a header first, then one row per day, with the date in ISO form and the day's revenue. The writer also takes care of quoting: if a value ever holds a comma, like the customer smith comma kim from day three, it is wrapped in quotes so it stays one column. The diagram on the right shows the move from a dictionary of dates to the rows of a file, and the terminal shows the result: head prints the first four lines, the header and the first three days, with the same totals the last course printed. The explorer shows the new folder, data slash out, with the report inside. Raw data comes in through data slash raw, and results go out through data slash out, and the program never writes into its own input. Next, making the numbers readable on screen.

The terminal output has so far been whatever print produced, with numbers wherever they happened to land. A report is easier to read when it lines up, and f-strings can do that with a format spec: a short code after a colon inside the braces. main dot py now prints a small table. Each row uses the same three specs. The product gets less than ten, which means left aligned in ten characters.
