The revenue gets greater than twelve comma dot two f, and the bags get greater than six. The pane on the right takes the revenue spec apart. The greater than sign aligns right. Twelve is the minimum width, so shorter values are padded with spaces. The comma adds a thousands separator. Dot two means two digits after the point, and the f means fixed point notation, an ordinary decimal number rather than scientific notation. Because every row uses the same widths, the columns line up, with text on the left and numbers on the right, which is how people read tables. The REPL shows a spec on its own. Square brackets around the result make the padding visible: four thousand four hundred sixty point nine becomes four spaces, then four comma four sixty point nine zero, exactly twelve characters. And the word KEN, left aligned in six, gets three spaces after it. The specs work on Decimal values too, so the money is never turned into a float just to print it. Formatting happens at the last moment, when a number becomes text for a person. The data underneath keeps its full precision, and only the display is rounded. Next, an output for programs instead of people.

A report is for people. The second output is for other programs: a summary the shop's website or another script can read. JSON is the standard for that, and the json module that read the catalogue can write too. json dot dumps turns Python values into JSON text. The diagram on the right shows how the types map. A dictionary becomes a JSON object, a string stays a string, integers and floats become numbers, lists and tuples become arrays, and None and True become null and true. Then there is one type JSON has no answer for: Decimal. Asked to dump a Decimal, json raises a TypeError, saying the object is not JSON serializable. That is a decision we have to make, and it matters. We could convert to float, but floats are exactly what the money has avoided since course four. And most programs read a JSON number back as a float, so even a correct number would be read inexactly. So write summary converts every amount to a string, with str, which writes the exact digits. The reader knows these fields are money and turns them back into Decimal. The function builds one dictionary: the month, the total, how many rows were rejected, and the revenue for each product, already ranked. A dictionary comprehension converts the revenue amounts. Then json dot dumps, with an indent of two to make the file readable, and write text saves it with UTF eight encoding. The terminal shows the start of the file. The total is in quotes, eleven thousand five hundred seventy eight point eight eight, exactly, and the rejected count is a plain number, because a count of rows is a whole number and needs no protecting. Next, a real database.

Files are fine for one month. But the shop will want to ask questions across many months, like how much Kenyan sold since spring, and that is what a database is for. Python ships with SQLite, a complete database stored in one file, in the sqlite3 module, so no server and no install are needed. At the top of the new code are three SQL statements kept as constants. The schema creates a table called order lines, if it does not already exist, with a column for each field, and the pane on the right lists them. The id is the primary key, so no two rows can share one. And the total is stored as whole cents in an integer column. Eleven thousand five hundred seventy eight point eight eight becomes one million one hundred fifty seven thousand eight hundred eighty eight cents, which every database stores exactly. load warehouse builds one tuple per line, then opens a connection. Used in a with block, a sqlite3 connection is a transaction. If the block finishes, everything is committed together, and if anything raises, everything is rolled back, so the table never holds half a month. Note that the with block does not close the connection, so the function closes it afterwards. executemany runs the insert once for each tuple, with question marks as placeholders. Never build SQL by pasting values into the string: placeholders let the database handle quoting, which is also what stops SQL injection. The first run prints a hundred and sixty three lines, and the total in cents. The second run fails, with an IntegrityError: the unique constraint on id. Every order is already there, so inserting it again is refused. The database is right to refuse, but the pipeline must be able to run twice. That is next.

A job that runs every night will one day run twice: someone re runs it after a failure, or a scheduler retries it. A pipeline is safe to re run when running it twice leaves the same result as running it once. The word for that is idempotent, and this step makes every output idempotent. The database first. The insert now carries an ON CONFLICT clause, making it what is called an upsert. If a row with that id already exists, the clause updates its fields in place, using excluded, which means the values we just tried to insert. The table at the bottom of the pane shows the difference on the second run: a plain insert raises an IntegrityError, and the upsert quietly updates. The terminal proves it. The job runs twice, and both runs report a hundred and sixty three lines and the same cents. Now the files. Writing a file takes time, and if the program crashes half way through, it leaves half a file, which the next reader would trust. write atomic avoids that. It writes the whole text to a temporary file next to the real one, then calls replace, which renames the temporary file over the real file in one step. The flow at the top of the pane shows it. Anyone reading summary dot json sees either the old file or the new one, never half of one. A crash before the rename leaves the old file untouched and a stray temporary file, and the next run simply writes it again. Both write report and write summary now build their text first and hand it to write atomic. ls lists data slash out: the report, the summary and the warehouse. Next, the whole job in one function.

Five courses ago, main dot py was two print calls. Now it is a complete pipeline, and this step gives it a front door. A function called main runs the whole job, in order. It finds the day files, sorted by date. It builds the priced lines, rejecting the bad rows, and keeps them in a list, because two steps need them: the summary and the warehouse. It summarises. Then it loads: the report, the summary and the warehouse. And it prints three facts: October's total, eleven thousand five hundred seventy eight eighty eight, a hundred and sixty three priced lines, and thirteen rejected rows. The last line of the file simply calls main. Wrapping the job in a function is a small change with a big reason: the file now defines things, and only the last line does anything, which course eight will build on. The side pane is the pipeline map from the first course, with every stage now lit, each one paired with the functions that do it. Extract is iter rows and read text, which read every day file one row at a time and survive the Latin one file. Validate is parse row and InvalidOrder, which refuse a line and say why. Transform is price line and priced lines, which apply the catalogue and the discount rules to the cent. Aggregate is summarise, one pass that answers every question. And load is write report, write summary and load warehouse, three outputs that are safe to write twice. Every one of those is plain Python from the standard library. That completes part one. The pipeline works. Part two makes it real: structured into a package, modelled with classes, tested, made fast and shipped on a schedule.

Part one ended with a pipeline that works, in one file of nearly two hundred lines. That is fine for one person on one afternoon, and painful for anyone who has to find something later. Part two makes the pipeline real, and the first step is to give it structure. A module is simply a Python file, and any file can import another. So the two extract functions, read text and iter rows, move out of main dot py into a new file, extract dot py, along with the csv import they need. main dot py gets one new line: from extract import iter rows. The program runs exactly as before, and the terminal shows the same October total. What does import actually do? The first time a module is imported, Python finds the file, runs it from top to bottom, and keeps the resulting module object in a dictionary called sys dot modules. Running extract dot py only defines two functions, so importing it is quick and has no side effects. Any later import of the same name finds it in sys dot modules and runs nothing. The REPL shows that entry: the key extract, and a module object that remembers which file it came from. The diagram on the right is the import graph so far: main imports extract. Python three fifteen adds a new word here: lazy. A lazy import binds the name immediately but loads the module only the first time the name is actually used. In the REPL, after lazy import sqlite3, sqlite3 is not yet in sys dot modules. Asking for its version loads it, and now it is. For a command line tool that only sometimes touches a heavy module, that makes starting up faster. Next, more than one module.

One module out of main dot py was a start. The pipeline has five stages, and each deserves a file of its own. When modules belong together, Python lets you put them in a folder and import them as a package. The new folder is called pipeline, and the file that marks it as a package is init dot py, with two underscores on each side. Here it holds only a docstring, but whatever it contains runs when the package is first imported. Inside are four modules, one per stage group. extract reads the files. validate holds the catalogue, InvalidOrder and parse row. transform prices lines and summarises the month. And load writes the three outputs. The old extract dot py at the top level is gone. main dot py shrinks to its imports, the two folder paths, and the main function. Its imports now name the package and the module, as in from pipeline dot load import write report. Inside the package, modules import each other with a leading dot. transform says from dot validate import, meaning the validate module next to me, so the package still works if it is renamed or moved. The REPL shows what one import pulls in. Importing pipeline dot transform loads three modules: the package itself first, then transform, then validate, because transform imports it. That is the graph drawn on the right. Now look at the first command in the terminal. We only asked Python to import main, to look at it, and the whole job ran: it read the month, and wrote all three outputs. Importing a file runs it, and main dot py still ends by calling main. A file that can be both run and imported needs one more line. That is next.

Every module has a name, stored in a variable called dunder name, short for double underscore name. When a file is imported, its name is the module's name, so importing main dot py gives it the name main. But when a file is run directly, as a script, Python gives it a special name instead: dunder main. The table at the top of the pane shows the two cases. That difference is what the last two lines of main dot py now check. If dunder name equals dunder main, call main. When you type python main dot py, the condition is true and the job runs, as the first command in the terminal shows. When another file, or a test, or you in the REPL, imports main, the condition is false, so the file only defines its names and the job does not run. The second command proves it: importing main and printing its name shows only the word main, and no report is written. And in the REPL, which is itself the main program, dunder name is dunder main. The flow on the right shows the shape every runnable Python file should have. The file runs from top to bottom, but everything above the guard is a definition: imports, constants and functions. Only the guard does anything, and only when the file is run as a script. You will see this idiom at the bottom of almost every Python script you read. It costs two lines, and it is what makes a script safe to import. That matters a great deal in course ten, where the tests import main and every function in the package, many times over, without ever wanting the job to run. Next, writing down what each function expects and returns.

Each function in the pipeline has a contract: what it expects, and what it gives back. So far those contracts lived in docstrings and in our heads. Type hints write them into the code. A hint follows a parameter after a colon, and the return type follows an arrow after the parentheses. to cents takes an amount, a Decimal, and returns a Decimal. Hints can describe containers too. iter rows takes an iterable of paths and returns an iterator of dictionaries mapping strings to strings. Long or repeated types get names. In validate, the type statement defines Row as a dictionary of strings, and Line as a dictionary of strings to any value. In transform, the summary gets something more precise: a TypedDict, which lists the eight keys a summary dictionary has, and the type of each. The pane on the right shows summarise as a typed box, lines in, Summary out, and the table beneath lists the contracts across the pipeline. Local variables can carry hints too, where Python cannot guess, like an empty Counter that will count strings. Here is the part that surprises people. Python itself does not check hints. It records them, and the REPL shows to cents' annotations: Decimal in, Decimal out. But calling to cents with a string is not stopped at the door. The call goes ahead, and fails one line later, inside the function, with an AttributeError, because a string has no quantize method. Hints are documentation that tools can read. Editors use them to complete names and to flag mistakes as you type. And a type checker reads every hint in the project, and compares it with how the code is actually used, without running anything. Next, we install one, and it finds a bug.

Everything so far has come from Python's standard library. A type checker does not, so this is the moment the project gets a proper description of itself. pyproject dot toml is the standard file for that. Its project table gives the name, a version, a description, and the Python it needs: three fifteen or later. A dependency group lists the tools a developer needs but the job does not, here mypy, pinned to an exact version, so everyone checks with the same rules. And a tool dot mypy table tells mypy which files to check: main dot py and the pipeline package. The flow on the right follows the chain. pip install, with the virtual environment active, puts mypy inside dot venv, never in the system's Python. Then mypy runs. It reads six files, and every hint in them, and executes nothing. It reports one error, in transform dot py, line eighty two. The TypedDict says the total is a Decimal. But the total comes from sum of totals, and mypy says that expression is a Decimal or the literal zero. Why? sum starts adding from the integer zero. The REPL shows it: the sum of an empty list is the int zero, not a Decimal. Our months have never been empty, so no run has shown it. But a month where every row was rejected would put an int into the summary where every other part of the pipeline expects exact money. The fix is a single argument: give sum a Decimal starting value, as the second REPL line does, and the answer is a Decimal zero. Course nine opens with that fix. This is what a type checker is for: it reads every path through the code, including the ones the test data never takes. The pipeline now has structure and contracts. Next, objects.

First, the fix from the end of the last course: summarise now gives sum a Decimal zero to start from, so an empty month is still exact money. Now, objects. Until now every piece of data in the pipeline has been a dictionary or a number. That works, but nothing stops a typo in a key, and the code that belongs to the data lives somewhere else. A class fixes both. It defines a new type: what data each object of that type carries, and what it can do. The new module, model dot py, holds the roastery's domain, and its first class is Product. The class statement names the type. Inside it, init, with two underscores on each side, is the method Python calls to fill in a new object. Its first parameter, self, is that new object, and the three assignments store the code, the name and the price on it. Those are attributes. The second method, cost, multiplies the price by a quantity. When you call kenya dot cost of three, Python passes kenya as self, so the method knows whose price to use. read catalogue now builds a Product for each coffee, and price line asks the product for its cost. The job still prints the same October total. The REPL looks at one product. Its name is Kenya Nyeri, its price is thirty one, and three bags cost ninety three. type of kenya is the class, pipeline dot model dot Product, and vars shows the attributes stored on the object itself. The diagram on the right draws that split: the name kenya points to an object holding its own data, and the object points to its class, which holds the methods every product shares. Data on the object, behaviour on the class. Next, a shorter way to write classes like this.

Product's init method did nothing but copy its arguments onto self, and most classes that hold data look exactly like that. The dataclasses module writes that code for you. Put the dataclass decorator above a class, list its fields with their types, and Python generates the init method, a readable repr, and an equality test that compares field by field. Product shrinks to three typed fields and its cost method. And the pipeline gets its most important type: LineItem, one valid order line. It has five fields: the order's id, its date, the customer, the Product, and the quantity. And it has one method of its own, total, which applies the discount rules and rounds to the cent. Those rules, and the rounding helper, moved into model dot py beside it. parse row now returns a LineItem instead of a dictionary, and the rest of the pipeline follows. Where summarise said line, square bracket, quoted quantity, it now says line dot quantity. That is more than tidier. A misspelt key in a dictionary is only found when that line runs; a misspelt attribute is flagged by an editor or by mypy before anything runs. The REPL builds a line by hand: four bags of the Brazilian coffee for Ana. Typing line alone shows the generated repr, every field by name, including the product inside it. Its total is sixty one seventy five: four bags at sixteen twenty five is sixty five, and that earns the five percent discount. And a line compares equal to a new LineItem built from the same fields, because the generated equality compares values, not identity. The pane on the right lists what the decorator wrote, and what you still write yourself. Next, rules a LineItem must never break.

An invariant is something that must be true of every object of a class, for its whole life. For a LineItem, one is obvious: nobody buys zero bags, or minus one. Until now that rule lived in parse row, as a check on the text. But a LineItem can be built anywhere, by a test or by a later course, so the rule belongs to the class itself. A dataclass lets you add a method called post init, which Python calls right after the generated init has set the fields. LineItem's post init checks the quantity, and if it is below one, raises a ValueError that says so. The REPL tries it: a line of zero bags is refused, and the traceback shows the path, from the call, through the generated init, into post init, and the message, quantity must be one or more, got zero. The flow on the right draws the same thing: every new LineItem passes through post init, and comes out either as a valid line, or as an error. parse row keeps the check that the quantity is made of digits, because text is its job, and it now catches the ValueError and turns it into InvalidOrder, so the rule is stated in one place only. The second change is smaller but just as useful. subtotal and total are now properties. The property decorator turns a method into something you read like an attribute, without parentheses. line dot total looks like data, but it is computed fresh each time from the product, the quantity and the discount. Nothing can fall out of step, because nothing is stored twice. Next, the money itself becomes an object.

Money has been Decimal since course four, which keeps it exact. But a Decimal does not know it is money. Nothing stops adding a price to a quantity, or storing an amount with five decimal places. A value object is a small class that wraps a value and knows its rules. Money is a frozen dataclass with one field, the amount. Frozen means its fields cannot be changed after it is made. Trying to assign a new amount raises a FrozenInstanceError. A Money is a value, like the number five: you never change it, you make a new one. That is exactly what the two methods do. Plus, written as dunder add, takes another Money and returns a new Money holding the sum. Times, dunder mul, multiplies by a quantity or a rate, and rounds to the cent, so the rounding rule lives inside the type now. Equality, hashing and the repr come from the frozen dataclass itself. The REPL shows all of it. a is nine ninety five, b is seventeen fifty. a plus b is a new Money of twenty seven forty five, a times three is twenty nine eighty five, and a itself is unchanged. The diagram on the right draws that: two names, two objects, and a third object that the addition made, with no name of its own. Two Money values with the same amount are equal, and because they hash the same, a set holding both keeps only one. Products now cost Money, line totals are Money, and summarise adds Money together. The summary prints, writes and loads exactly as before, because Money's str is just its amount. Next, a class that holds many objects.

The valid lines and the rejected rows have travelled through the pipeline as two separate things: a generator, and a list passed in to be filled. They belong together, so they become one object, Orders, in validate dot py. Its init takes the lines and the rejected rows. But nobody wants to build those lists by hand. They want to say: here are the rows, give me the orders. That is an alternate constructor, written as a class method. The classmethod decorator passes the class itself as the first argument, called cls, instead of an object. from rows loops over the rows, parses each one, collects the lines and the rejections, and finishes by calling cls with both lists. Why cls and not Orders by name? Because a subclass of Orders would then build itself correctly too. The other three methods let Orders work with Python's own syntax. len of orders calls dunder len. A for loop over orders calls dunder iter, which hands back an iterator over the lines. And the in operator calls dunder contains, which checks the order ids. The table on the right pairs each piece of syntax with the method it calls. The REPL asks all three. There are a hundred and sixty three lines. ORD one thousand and one is in the orders. ORD one thousand and thirteen is not, because it was rejected for having no customer. main dot py shrinks to match: Orders from rows, then summarise the orders, then write them out. The priced lines generator is gone, and so is the rejected list that had to be passed in. Special methods like these are how a class of your own becomes as natural to use as a list. Next, the errors get a family.

Every refused row so far has been one kind of error, InvalidOrder, with a message. But the shop treats them differently. A row with a missing customer is a typing slip at the till. A row naming a product the catalogue does not sell may mean the catalogue is out of date. A program that wants to react differently needs different types, and inheritance lets them share a parent. The new module errors dot py starts with PipelineError, a subclass of Exception: the parent of everything the pipeline refuses. InvalidRow inherits from it, for missing and malformed fields, and adds nothing but its name and docstring. UnknownProduct inherits from it too, and adds something: the product code that was not found. Its init takes the row id and the code, builds the message, and hands that message to the parent with super dot init. super means: the same method, in my parent class. So Exception still stores the message as it always does, and UnknownProduct only adds what is new, the sku attribute. validate now raises the specific type, and Orders catches PipelineError, so it still collects both kinds. The diagram on the right is the family tree, and the table beside it is the rule that makes it useful: an except clause catches the class it names, and every subclass of it. Catching PipelineError catches both. Catching UnknownProduct catches only the missing coffees. The REPL counts the October rejections by type: nine invalid rows, and four unknown products, all of them GUA two fifty, a Guatemalan coffee the catalogue does not list yet. Now the shop can tell the two apart, and fix each at its source. Next, inheritance for behaviour, not just for names.

The discount rules have lived in one function since course four, as an if, an elif and a default. Every new promotion would mean another branch in the same function. Polymorphism offers another shape: many classes that answer the same question, each in its own way. DiscountRule is the base class. It has a rate, zero by default, and a method, applies, that takes a line and answers yes or no. On the base class, applies just raises NotImplementedError: it is a promise that subclasses must keep. Bulk keeps it by answering yes for ten or more bags, at fifteen percent. Wholesale answers yes for a line worth fifty or more, at five percent. And NoDiscount always answers yes, at zero. RULES lists one of each, in priority order. LineItem gets a new property, rule, which asks each rule in turn and takes the first one that says yes. And total simply multiplies the subtotal by one minus that rule's rate. Look at what total no longer knows. It does not know how many rules exist, or what any of them check. It calls applies on each, and each object runs its own version. That is polymorphism: one call, many behaviours, chosen by the object's class. The if and elif from course four are gone. A new promotion is a new class with its own applies, added to RULES, and nothing else changes. The REPL counts which rule priced each October line: eighty four lines paid full price, forty five got the wholesale discount, and thirty four got the bulk discount. The diagram on the right shows one question and three answers. The October total is still eleven thousand five hundred seventy eight eighty eight, to the cent. Next, two ways to describe what a class must provide.

The pipeline reads from one place and writes to three. If those were described by what they can do, rather than what they are, any of them could be replaced: a test could read from a list, or write into memory. Python offers two ways to describe such a contract. The first is a Protocol, from the typing module. ports dot py defines two. A Source is anything with a rows method that returns an iterator of rows. A Sink is anything with a write method that takes a result. The three dots are the whole body: a protocol only describes a shape. The classes that fit it do not inherit from it, or even import it. CsvDays in extract has a rows method, so it is a Source. CsvReport and JsonSummary in load have write methods, so they are Sinks. This is structural typing, and the dashed edges on the right show it: they match the shape, without any family tie. Result is a small dataclass bundling the orders and the summary, which is what every sink receives. main dot py now names its source and its list of sinks, and mypy checks that each really fits: nine files, no issues. The second way is an abstract base class, an ABC. DiscountRule now inherits from ABC, and its applies method is marked abstractmethod. That is nominal typing: subclasses must inherit from it, and they must fill in every abstract method. Python enforces it when an object is made. The REPL tries to create a bare DiscountRule, and gets a TypeError: it cannot instantiate an abstract class without an implementation for applies. Use an ABC when you own a family of classes and want each to finish the job. Use a Protocol when you only care that something has the right methods. Next, the warehouse cleans up after itself.

In course seven, a with block around a database connection gave us a transaction: commit if the block finished, roll back if it raised. Any class can offer that, by being a context manager. SqliteWarehouse in load dot py is the warehouse as a Sink, and it has the two methods that make with work. dunder enter runs when the block begins. It makes sure the output folder exists, connects, creates the table if needed, and returns the warehouse, which with binds to the name after as. That folder line matters: main now opens the warehouse first, before the report has created data slash out, and without it a first run on a clean checkout fails, unable to open the database file. dunder exit runs when the block ends, however it ends. Python passes it three arguments describing an exception, or three Nones if there was none. So exit commits if the kind is None, rolls back otherwise, and closes the connection either way. Because it returns nothing, an exception carries on outwards after the rollback, and the program still learns about it. The flow on the right draws both paths. The terminal proves the bad one. The warehouse already holds October from a run of main. Inside a with block, the REPL deletes every row, and asks for the totals: zero rows. Then it raises an error, on purpose, carrying that count as its message. Exit sees the exception and rolls back. Afterwards, Python's own sqlite3 command line counts the rows again: a hundred and sixty three, all still there. The deletion never happened, as far as anyone outside the block can tell. That is the guarantee a context manager gives: setup and cleanup, paired, on every path. Next, the parts become one pipeline.

The model is complete: products, lines, money, orders, errors, rules, sources and sinks. The last step puts them together, and the way it does so matters. Pipeline, in run dot py, is a dataclass with two fields: a source, and a list of sinks. Its run method is the whole job in four lines. It builds the orders from the source's rows, summarises them into a result, hands the result to every sink, and returns it. Pipeline inherits from nothing. It has a source and has sinks, rather than being a kind of either. That is composition: building behaviour by combining parts, instead of extending parents. The REPL confirms it: Pipeline's method resolution order is Pipeline, then object, the root of every class, and nothing else. The diagram on the right draws the has a edges. main dot py now reads like a description of the job. Open the warehouse. Build a Pipeline from the day files in the raw folder, and three sinks: the CSV report, the JSON summary, and the warehouse. Run it, read the warehouse totals, and print. The terminal shows the same October as ever, eleven thousand five hundred seventy eight eighty eight, a hundred and sixty three lines and thirteen rejected, and mypy checks all ten files without an issue. Why prefer composition? Because parts can be swapped without touching anything else. A test can give Pipeline a fake source holding three made up rows, and a plain list as its sink, and check exactly what arrived. Next month's job could add a fourth sink, or read from the shop's web API, and Pipeline would not change a line. That swapping is exactly what the next course does. The pipeline is modelled. Now we make it trustworthy.

Every course so far has checked the pipeline the same way: run it, and look at the October total. That catches a lot, but only for October, and only when someone looks. A test is code that checks code, and runs in a second, every time anything changes. pytest is the standard tool, so it joins mypy in the project's development dependencies, pinned to an exact version, and pip install with the group option installs everything that group lists. pytest's rules are simple. It looks in the tests folder for files whose names start with test, and inside them, for functions whose names start with test. Each test is an ordinary function that uses a plain assert. If every assert holds, the test passes. If one fails, pytest reports which, and shows the values involved. The first file, test model dot py, checks the model from the last course. Adding two Money values gives a new value and leaves the first unchanged. Multiplying rounds to the cent. And each discount rule is checked at its edge. Ten bags of Kenyan coffee get the bulk rule, and come to two hundred sixty three fifty. Two bags come to sixty two, which earns the wholesale discount, fifty eight ninety. One bag pays full price. Every one of those numbers can be worked out by hand, which is the point. The flow on the right shows the shape of a good test: arrange the inputs, act by calling the code under test, and assert what must be true. pytest dash q runs all five: five dots, five passed. Collect only lists the tests it found, by file and name, and the names read like a specification of the rules. Next, sharing set up between tests, and running one test many times.

Tests repeat themselves. Every rule test built the same Kenyan product, and the validation tests will all need a valid row to start from. pytest's answer is a fixture: a function marked with the fixture decorator, which builds something a test needs. A test asks for a fixture simply by naming it as a parameter, and pytest calls the fixture and passes in the result, fresh for every test, so no test can spoil another's data. Fixtures that many test files share live in conftest dot py, which pytest loads automatically. There are two so far: kenya, a product at thirty one a bag, and good row, a valid CSV row for two bags of it. The rule tests now take kenya instead of a module constant. test validate dot py starts with the happy path: a good row becomes a line of two bags. Then the interesting part. There are five ways the October data was refused, and writing five near identical tests would bury the idea in repetition. parametrize runs one test once for each set of arguments. Each case names a field to break, the bad value, and the error it must raise: no customer, a quantity in words, a negative quantity, zero bags, and an unknown product. The test copies the good row, changes that one field, and uses pytest dot raises to assert that parse row refuses it with exactly that kind of error. Each case gets a readable id, and collect only lists them, one test fanned out into five. The diagram on the right draws that: the fixture flows into the test, and the test into its cases. The whole suite is now eleven tests, all passing. Next, testing the pipeline without its files.

Testing the whole pipeline the obvious way would mean thirty one CSV files, a SQLite database and a folder of outputs, for every test. The protocols from the last course make that unnecessary. A test double is an object that stands in for a real part during a test. FakeSource has a rows method that serves rows from a list, so it fits the Source protocol exactly as CsvDays does, with no base class and no change to the pipeline. ListSink has a write method that keeps every result it is handed, so it fits Sink. The diagram on the right shows the two sources, one real and one fake, both fitting the same shape. There is one more part that makes runs hard to test: time. This step adds a generated timestamp to every summary, so the JSON records when it was made. Read from the real clock, it changes on every run, and no test could assert it. So Pipeline takes the clock as a part too. By default it is utc now, which reads the real time. The test passes a small lambda that always answers noon on the thirty first of October. The test builds a pipeline from a fake source holding one good row and one refused row, a list sink, and the fixed clock, then runs it. It asserts that the sink received exactly the result, that there is one line and one rejection, that the total is fifty eight ninety, and that the timestamp is noon. No file was read and nothing was written. The terminal runs the suite, twelve passed, then the real job, which writes a real timestamp, and mypy confirms the new clock part is typed correctly. Use doubles only at the edges like this: files, networks, clocks. Next, telling the operator what happened.

The pipeline talks to its operator with print. That is fine on a laptop, but a scheduled job runs with nobody watching, and print has no way to say how important a message is, or to be switched off. The logging module does both. Each module asks for its own logger with getLogger of dunder name, so every message carries where it came from. extract now logs the Latin one notice as a warning instead of printing it. validate logs each refused row at debug level, the lowest. And main logs the month's total and the files written at info level. Messages travel through a small chain, drawn on the right. The logger creates a record. A handler decides where records go, and drops those below its level. A formatter turns a record into a line of text. You rarely build that chain by hand. One call to basicConfig, at the start of main, creates a single handler that writes to standard error, with the format level, logger name, colon, message. Its level comes from an environment variable, LOG LEVEL, and defaults to info. The first run shows three lines, each labelled with its level and its source: a warning from pipeline dot extract, and two info lines from main. The debug records were created but dropped, because debug is below info. The second run sets LOG LEVEL to debug, and the refused rows appear, each with its reason, interleaved with the warning in the order they happened. The operator chooses how much to see, without anyone editing the code. The tests still pass, because the library code only creates records, and only main decides what happens to them. That split matters: a library should log, and only the application configures. Next, functions that wrap functions.

You have used decorators since the model course: dataclass, property, classmethod. This step writes two, and shows what the at sign actually does. timed, in decorators dot py, logs how long each call takes. It is a function that takes a function and returns a new one. Inside, it defines wrapper, which starts a clock, calls the original function with whatever arguments it was given, and in a finally block, so even a failing call is timed, logs the name and the seconds. timed returns wrapper. Writing at timed above def run is exactly the same as writing run equals timed of run. So Pipeline dot run is now the wrapper. How does the wrapper still find the original run, long after timed has returned? Through a closure. A function defined inside another keeps the variables it uses from the enclosing call alive, in cells attached to it. The REPL looks inside: Pipeline dot run's closure holds one cell, and its contents are the original function, Pipeline dot run. The diagram on the right draws the name, the wrapper and the cell. functools dot wraps copies the original's name and docstring onto the wrapper, so tracebacks and logs still say run, not wrapper. The terminal shows the new info line: Pipeline dot run took a few hundredths of a second. retry is a decorator with arguments, so it is one level deeper: retry, called with the error to catch and the number of attempts, returns the real decorator. Its wrapper calls the function, logs and tries again on that error, and lets the last attempt fail for real. Two new tests prove it: a flaky function succeeds on its third call, and a broken one still raises. Course eleven uses retry on a network source. Next, finding a bug.

A new test checks summarise on two lines simple enough to work out by hand: one bag of Ethiopian at nine ninety five, and one bag of Kenyan at thirty one. The total should be forty ninety five, and the median, halfway between the two, is twenty point four seven five, which rounds to twenty forty eight. The test fails. Rather than scattering print calls, put one line where you want to look: breakpoint. It is built into Python, and when execution reaches it, it opens pdb, the Python debugger, right there, with every local variable available. The line goes into summarise, just after the amounts are collected, and pytest runs the new test. pytest notices the breakpoint, turns off its output capturing, and pdb shows where it stopped: transform dot py, in summarise, at the breakpoint. At the pdb prompt, p prints any expression. The median of the amounts is Decimal twenty point four seven five: three decimal places. Up moves one frame towards the caller, into the test, at the line that called summarise. Down would move back. The stack on the right shows those two frames. Now the bug is clear, and it is not in summarise at all. Money promises whole cents, but only its multiply method rounded. The median of two amounts is their average, and that half a cent slipped straight into a Money, which then compares unequal to twenty forty eight. On October's real data the median happened to be a single line, so every run looked right. A breakpoint is temporary: q quits the debugger, and the line must not stay in the code. The note at the bottom says where the fix belongs: in Money itself, so that no caller, now or later, can make one with part of a cent. That fix comes next, with one more kind of check.

First, the fix from the debugger. The breakpoint is gone, and Money has a post init method that rounds its amount to the cent, whatever it was given. Because the dataclass is frozen, it sets the field with object dot setattr, the one sanctioned way round frozen during construction. Multiply no longer rounds by itself, because every Money now does, and the median test passes. Tests check behaviour. Two more kinds of check cover what tests do not: mistakes visible in the code itself, and its layout. ruff does both, and joins the development dependencies. ruff check is a linter. It reads the code, without running it, against hundreds of rules, each with a code. Here it finds four real problems, listed on the right by rule. F four oh one: transform still imports Decimal, which nothing there uses since Money took over. RUF oh five nine: main unpacks the warehouse's cents and never uses them. PYI oh three four: SqliteWarehouse's enter method should be typed as returning Self, so subclasses keep their type. And FURB one five seven: Decimal of the string zero is just Decimal of zero. ruff marks the ones it can fix itself, and the others are a moment's work by hand; they are done before the next course begins. ruff format is a formatter. pyproject sets the line length to seventy nine, the limit from Python's style guide, and the formatter rewrites nine files to one consistent layout. Nobody argues about where a bracket goes, because the tool decides. The tests still pass, fifteen of them, because formatting changes layout and never behaviour. Linter, formatter, type checker and tests: four checks, all automatic, run on every change. The pipeline is now trustworthy. Next, we make it fast.
